_readme: Mission Tutor dialogue. Edit freely. {placeholders} are filled from the live mission (see TutorDialogueManager.context()). Steps advance when 'until' happens: next (Enter), move, open:<screen>, close, focus_part, pick, adcs, launch, event:<name>.

say: Welcome aboard, Mission Director. Today we're sending a satellite into space to help farmers protect their crops.
Floods can ruin a whole season of crops in a few days. From space, we can spot them early and warn people in time.
But we have only ${budget} million and our satellite can weigh at most {mass_limit} kg. Every choice has a price.
Turn around and look through the big window behind you: that's our rocket, waiting on the launch pad.
First, let's look around. Use W, A, S, D to walk and the mouse to look.
Every mission starts with a promise: what the satellite must do. Ours is on the BRIEFING screen. Follow the yellow arrow and press E.
We promised three things. First: see each farm area at least every {max_revisit} days, because floods move fast.
Second: send home {min_data} GB of useful pictures every day. Third: keep working for at least {min_life} years.
Press E to close the screen when you're ready.
These shelves hold real spacecraft parts. Look at one to see what it costs in weight, power and money.
steps.todo: Look at a part on a shelf

say: Every slot has a simple, cheap option and a better, pricier one. We start with the simple ones.
Before you commit, the DECISION card on the right shows what would change. Green is better, amber is a warning sign, red means trouble. Press E to install a part.
Keep an eye on LAUNCH CONTROL on the left. It's our dashboard: money, weight, and whether the rocket can carry us.
Here's something important: power. Our solar panels only work in sunlight, and for about {eclipse} minutes of every {period}-minute orbit, Earth blocks the Sun.
During that darkness, the battery keeps everything alive. Think of a phone running on its battery all night.
Now the pictures. Our camera makes {data_gen} GB a day, but basic pointing keeps only {pointing_pct}% of them sharp.
That's just {useful} GB of useful pictures a day, and we promised {min_data}. A blurry photo of a flood helps nobody.
Let's fix that. Walk to the POINTING shelf and install the precision attitude control. It costs a bit more power and weight, but every picture comes out sharp.
Our engineers report on the ADVISORS screen. If something is going to break, they'll tell you there. Go and have a look.
Now we choose our ride to space. Our rocket has limited carrying capacity. Think of it like packing a suitcase: carry too much and we need a bigger, more expensive rocket.
Head to the MISSION CONSOLE on the right wall. That's where we pick our orbit and our rocket.
{orbit_lines}
Take a look at your options. Every choice has a price. When LAUNCH CONTROL says READY, press LAUNCH.
We made it! Look out of the window: that's Africa, right beneath us.
Those glowing rings are our four farming regions. The little squares inside are the fields we care about.
But here's the problem: our satellite doesn't have unlimited power or memory, and it only passes over Africa now and then. We must choose carefully.
Walk to the OBSERVATION CONSOLE on the left wall. It shows which regions are below us right now.
Pick a region marked IN VIEW, then press SCAN. Watch the SATELLITE CAMERA on the right wall zoom in.
Careful with clouds: our camera sees light, like your phone camera. Thick cloud means white pictures.
Every scan uses one pass and fills our memory. Try to photograph all four regions at least once.
When you've done what you can, press END OBSERVATION CAMPAIGN. Everything we stored goes to Level 3.
steps.todo: Scan the regions, then end the campaign

say: Welcome to the ground station! We've got {collected} GB of pictures waiting up there.
But there's a catch. The satellite can only talk to us while it flies over these dishes, for about {contact} minutes a day.
Imagine trying to send ten big videos through a very slow internet connection. That's what our satellite is dealing with.
GROUND CONTROL on the left shows the bottleneck: what's onboard against what the link can carry.
Choose what comes down first with the PRIORITY buttons on the middle desk: flood pictures or crop pictures. Then press START PASS and watch the sky.
steps.todo: Set a priority, then press START PASS

say: Here it comes! See the dishes turning to follow it? That green line is our radio link. Every dot is a packet of pictures.
The data has finally reached Earth: {received} GB of it. But collecting pictures is only half the job.
Look out of the window: those are the very farms our satellite photographed. Some fields are green, some are yellowing, some are under water.
Now we need to turn pictures into help for the farmers.
Go to the ANALYSIS WORKSTATION on the left wall. Grey squares are places we have no pictures of: we can't know what's happening there.
Click every plot that looks flooded (blue). Then choose how to tell people, and press DELIVER REPORT. Remember: a flood alert is only useful if it arrives in time.
steps.todo: Mark the flooded plots and deliver

concepts.payload: This is the camera, the reason we're going to space. Sharper or richer pictures are great, but they make bigger files.
concepts.solar: Solar panels are our only power source. No sunlight, no power: that's what the battery is for.
concepts.battery: The battery is our power bank for the dark side of each orbit. We only drain it part way, so it lasts for years.
concepts.comms: The radio is our link home. It can only talk while a ground station is in view, so a faster radio sends more in the same time.
concepts.computer: The computer is the satellite's brain, and it stores pictures until the next chance to send them.
concepts.adcs: Attitude control keeps the camera pointed at the ground. Think of trying to take a photo from a spinning car.
concepts.propulsion: A thruster lets us change or hold our orbit. It's handy, but it's heavy and can be very power-hungry.
concepts.thermal: In space it swings from scorching sunlight to freezing shadow every orbit. Blankets keep the heat in for free; heaters cost power.

reactions.say: Excellent detail! But sharper pictures usually mean larger files: {data_gen} GB a day now. Let's make sure our radio can send them home.
The multispectral camera makes smaller files. Easier to send home, but less science in each picture.
X-band! That's like upgrading from slow home internet to fibre. It does use more power while it talks.
The S-band radio is cheap and light, but it's a narrow pipe. Fine for small pictures, not for big ones.
Bigger solar wings: about twice the power. Great for hungry parts, but they add weight.
Body panels are light and simple, but they don't make much power. Keep the power-hungry parts in check.
A bigger battery is like packing a large power bank. We'll get through every eclipse with energy to spare.
Excellent decision! Every picture will now come out sharp. You've protected the most important part of our mission.
Careful: with basic pointing, more than half of our pictures will come out blurry.
The ion thruster is powerful but very hungry: it needs 10 watts. Watch the power.
Heaters keep the battery cosy, but they eat 4 watts of power, all the time.
A smarter computer with more memory. It also uses almost 4 watts.
A rocket all to ourselves! But at ${rocket_cost} million it costs more than our whole budget.
You've saved money. Good thinking! We share the ride with other satellites, so it's cheap, but we go where the rocket goes.
Sun-synchronous orbit: we pass over the farms every {revisit} days, always at the same time of day. Ground contact is a little shorter, though.
This lower orbit is easy to reach, but we'd only see the farms every {revisit} days. Floods move faster than that.
The rocket can't carry us! We need a lighter satellite or a bigger rocket.
We're running out of money. A mission that goes over budget gets cancelled.
We're nearly too heavy. Every extra kilogram is a risk.
We have a problem: our parts need more power than the panels can make. Something will have to switch off.
The battery can't get us through the dark side of each orbit. We'd go into safe mode in every eclipse.
We have a problem. Not all our data can reach Earth. Which pictures matter most? A faster radio would help.
Excellent decision! We'll now deliver enough useful pictures every day.
Now we'll see the farms often enough to catch floods in time. Well done!
Power is back in the green. Everything can run at once.
Our radio can now send home everything the camera makes.
We can't launch like this. Check LAUNCH CONTROL on the left: something is over the limit.
We can launch, but the mission will struggle. Press LAUNCH again only if you're sure.
Look at those fields! That pass made {scan_gb} GB of pictures. Memory used: {stored} of {storage} GB.
Clouds! Our camera can't see through thick cloud, so that pass gave us mostly white pictures. Try that region again on another pass.
Our memory is filling up: {stored} of {storage} GB. In the next level all of this has to squeeze through a narrow radio link.
Memory full! New pictures are being lost. More storage or fewer scans would have helped.
That was our last pass this month. Time to end the campaign and send the pictures home.
That region isn't below us right now. Wait for the next pass over Africa: the console shows when it's IN VIEW.
Floods first. If the link runs out of time, the crop pictures are the ones that wait.
Crop health first. Good for long-term planning, but a flood warning could arrive late.
The pass is over and the link has closed. {left_onboard} GB never made it down. That's the data bottleneck: more data than our link can carry.
Excellent! Everything we collected reached Earth before the satellite flew out of range.
First choose how to tell people: an emergency alert, a flood map, a crop report or a dashboard.
An emergency alert goes straight to farmers' phones. Perfect for floods, as long as it's on time.
A flood risk map helps officials decide where to send help first.
A crop report is great for planning the season, but too slow for a flood emergency.
A dashboard keeps everyone updated, but someone has to be watching it.
Report sent! You found {flood_found} of {flood_total} flooded plots and warned people in time. That's a mission that helps farmers.
Report sent. You found {flood_found} of {flood_total} flooded plots. Some help arrives, but not all of it.
Report sent, but it won't help much: only {flood_found} of {flood_total} flooded plots found.
{unseen_flood} flooded plots were in the grey areas. Nobody warned those farmers, because the pictures never reached us.
